sentence_zh: 狗子還有佛性也無？州云：無。
sentence_pinyin: Gǒuzi hái yǒu fúxìng yě wú? Zhōu yún: Wú.

translators.work: No Barrier: Unlocking the Zen Koan (1993)
translators.text: Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou said, 'No.'
translators.notes: Direct negative, focusing on cutting off the discursive question.

translators.text: Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said: 'Wu!'
translators.notes: Preserves Chinese 'Wu' while noting its function as a diamond sword severing duality.

translators.work: The Record of Linji & Zen Commentary
translators.text: Does even a dog have Buddha-nature, or not? Jōshū said: 'Mu!'
translators.notes: Preserves the Japanese/Chinese untranslated sacred syllable Mu (無).

translators.text: Has a dog Buddha-nature? Chao-chou replied: 'Wu!'
translators.notes: Emphasizes Wu as the living spirit beyond intellectual affirmative or negative.

translators.text: A monk once asked Joshu, "Has a dog the Buddha-nature?" Joshu answered, "Mu!"
translators.notes: VERIFIED verbatim vs the Mark T. Morse illustrated reproduction of Blyth's translation (Zen and Zen Classics IV, Hokuseido Press 1966). Retains 'Mu' untranslated with Hokuseido-era spellings (Joshu, Buddha-nature).

source.work: Zen and Zen Classics, Volume Four: Mumonkan, tr. R.H. Blyth
source.edition: Hokuseido Press, 1966 — text per the Mark T. Morse illustrated reproduction (gatelessgatestudio.com, which states it uses Blyth verbatim)
source.note: Replaces a prior near-verbatim paraphrase ('asked' for 'once asked'; hyphenation).
source.gloss: Blyth adds: '(Mu is the negative symbol in Chinese, meaning No-thing or Nay.)'

translators.work: The Zen Teaching of Zen Masters
translators.text: Has a dog Buddha-nature or not? The Master replied: 'None!'
translators.notes: Translates as 'None', emphasizing emptiness of inherent fixed nature.

translators.text: A monk asked: 'Does a dog possess Buddha-nature?' Zhaozhou replied: 'Mu / Not.'
translators.notes: Provides glossing of 狗子 (diminutive/vernacular for dog) and 無 (as categorical ungraspability).

translators.text: Joshu answered: "Mu."
translators.notes: VERIFIED verbatim vs Wikisource/sacred-texts (1934 John Murray edition, non-renewed → public domain). Retains 'Mu' untranslated — the register that defined the case for Western readers.

source.work: The Gateless Gate, tr. Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps
source.edition: John Murray, Los Angeles, 1934 — public domain (non-renewal)

sentence_zh: 至道無難，唯嫌揀擇。但莫憎愛，洞然明白。
sentence_pinyin: Zhì dào wú nán, wéi xián jiǎnzé. Dàn mò zēng ài, dòng rán míng bái.

translators.work: The Zen Teaching of Bodhidharma & Early Masters
translators.text: The Great Way is not hard, it only detests picking and choosing. Simply without hate or love, it opens wide and clear.
translators.notes: Renders 洞然明白 as 'opens wide and clear', emphasizing the spatial awakening.

translators.text: The Great Way is not difficult, it only avoids picking and choosing. Just do not love or hate, and it is clearly evident.
translators.notes: Renders 揀擇 as 'picking and choosing', 洞然 as 'clearly evident'.

translators.text: The Great Way is not difficult, for those who have no preferences. When love and hate are both absent, everything becomes clear and undisguised.
translators.notes: Renders 揀擇 as 'having no preferences', captures universal non-attachment.

translators.text: The Perfect Way knows no difficulties, except that it refuses to make preferences. Only when freed from hate and love, it reveals itself fully and without disguise.
translators.notes: Flowing poetic structure, standard in Western zendo chanting.

translators.text: The supreme Way is not difficult, only dislike choosing. Just have neither hatred nor love, and all will be lucid and clear.
translators.notes: Faithful to Chinese word order and grammatical structure.

sentence_zh: 赤肉團上有一無位真人，常從諸人面門出入。未證據者看看！
sentence_pinyin: Chì ròu tuán shàng yǒu yī wú wèi zhēn rén, cháng cóng zhū rén miàn mén chū rù. Wèi zhèng jù zhě kàn kàn!

translators.work: The Zen Teaching of the Ancestors
translators.text: On this lump of red flesh is a True Person without rank, constantly going in and out through the gates of your face. You who haven't witnessed it: look, look!
translators.notes: Translates 面門 as 'gates of your face' and 無位真人 as 'True Person without rank'.

translators.text: On your lump of red flesh is a True Person of No Rank who is constantly going in and out through your facial gates. Those who have not yet recognized him: look, look!
translators.notes: Standard academic translation of 無位真人 as 'True Person of No Rank'.

translators.text: On this lump of red flesh is a true human of no status, constantly entering and exiting through the gates of your face. Those who have not experienced this, look! Look!
translators.notes: Renders 真人 as 'true human' and 無位 as 'no status'.

translators.text: In this lump of red meat there is a True Man of No Title, always entering and leaving through your senses. Look at him, you who have not yet seen him!
translators.notes: Uses 'True Man of No Title' and 'senses' for 面門 (facial gates).

sentence_zh: 菩提本無樹，明鏡亦非臺。本來無一物，何處惹塵埃。
sentence_pinyin: Pútí běn wú shù, míngjìng yì fēi tái. Běnlái wú yī wù, héchù rě chén'āi.

translators.work: The Platform Sutra: The Zen Teaching of Hui-neng (2006)
translators.text: Bodhi originally has no tree, the mirror has no stand. From the beginning not a thing exists; where could dust ever alight?
translators.notes: Red Pine's celebrated translation highlighting Dunhuang vs. Dexin woodblock variations.

translators.work: The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch (1967)
translators.text: Bodhi fundamentally has no tree, the bright mirror also has no stand. Fundamentally there is not a single thing: where could any dust alight?
translators.notes: Based on the Dunhuang manuscript transmission.

translators.text: Bodhi fundamentally has no tree, nor is the clear mirror a stand. Originally there is not a single thing; where could dust gather?
translators.notes: Clean, unembellished rendering of the classic quadrain.

translators.text: Bodhi originally has no tree in it, nor has the mind-mirror any stand in it; originally there is not a single thing: Where can any dust gather?
translators.notes: Emphasizes the absolute Emptiness (śūnyatā) of original nature.
